summary.text: Explicit decimal-carry formulas on each block of 100 terms, together with columnwise uniqueness and finite checks for small prefix digit sums, show that every block contains at least nine occurrences of 8 while any fixed other value occurs at most nine times. Summing over complete blocks and bounding the incomplete tail gives asymptotic upper bounds of \(9/100\) for all competitors and a lower bound of \(9/100\) for 8, hence the limsup comparison.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
s(n)=\text{the sum of the decimal digits of }n,
\qquad
a(n)=s(n)\bmod s(n+1),
\]
where the remainder is the least nonnegative remainder. For \(N,m\in\mathbb N\), put
\[
C_m(N)=\#\{0\le n<N:a(n)=m\}.
\]
We prove that for every \(m\),
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_m(N)}N
\le
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_8(N)}N.
\]
The proof is based on a uniform comparison within each block of 100 consecutive integers.

First, we record the elementary digit-sum formulas that will be used. If \(q\ge0\), \(0\le t<10\), and \(0\le u<10\), then appending the two decimal digits \(t,u\) to \(q\), allowing leading zeroes among those final two positions, gives
\[
s(100q+10t+u)=s(q)+t+u. \tag{1}
\]
This is also valid for \(q=t=u=0\), since both sides are zero.

Suppose first that \(u<9\). There is no carry into the tens digit when 1 is added, so by (1)
\[
s(100q+10t+u+1)=s(q)+t+u+1.
\]
The numerator is strictly smaller than this denominator, and therefore
\[
a(100q+10t+u)=s(q)+t+u. \tag{2}
\]
If instead \(u=9\) and \(t<9\), adding 1 changes the last two digits from \(t9\) to \((t+1)0\). Hence
\[
a(100q+10t+9)
=(s(q)+t+9)\bmod(s(q)+t+1). \tag{3}
\]
Since
\[
s(q)+t+9=(s(q)+t+1)+8,
\]
formula (3) shows in particular that whenever \(s(q)+t\ge8\),
\[
a(100q+10t+9)=8. \tag{4}
\]
If \(s(q)+t<8\), the value in (3), being a remainder modulo \(s(q)+t+1\), is less than 8.

We now analyze the first 99 positions of a block. Write
\[
x=s(q).
\]
For \(0\le r<99\), define \(V_x(r)\) by writing \(r=10t+u\), where \(0\le u<10\), and setting
\[
V_x(10t+u)=
\begin{cases}
x+t+u,&u<9,\\
(x+t+9)\bmod(x+t+1),&u=9.
\end{cases} \tag{5}
\]
For \(r<99\), the case \(u=9\) only occurs with \(0\le t\le8\). Equations (2) and (3) give
\[
a(100q+r)=V_{s(q)}(r)\qquad(0\le r<99). \tag{6}
\]

We need three counting facts about the values \(V_x(r)\) for \(0\le r<99\).

First, if \(m<8\), then
\[
\#\{0\le r<99:V_x(r)=m\}\le8. \tag{7}
\]
For \(x\ge8\), this is immediate from (5): when \(u<9\), the value is \(x+t+u\ge8\), while when \(u=9\), equation (4) says that the value is exactly 8. Thus no value below 8 occurs at all.

It remains only to check \(0\le x\le7\). Substituting \(r=10t+u\) into (5) gives the following table. Row \(x\) lists, in order, the exact numbers of occurrences of \(m=0,1,\ldots,7\) among \(r=0,1,\ldots,98\):
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
x\backslash m&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
0&5&3&5&5&5&6&7&8\\
1&3&2&4&4&4&5&6&7\\
2&2&1&3&3&3&4&5&6\\
3&2&1&1&2&2&3&4&5\\
4&1&1&1&1&1&2&3&4\\
5&1&1&1&0&0&1&2&3\\
6&1&1&0&0&0&0&1&2\\
7&1&0&0&0&0&0&0&1
\end{array}
\]
This is a direct finite calculation from (5): for each \(r\), use \(x+t+u\) in the nine columns \(u=0,\ldots,8\), and use \((x+t+9)\bmod(x+t+1)\) in the column \(u=9\), with \(t=0,\ldots,8\) in that last column. Every displayed entry is at most 8, proving (7).

Second, if \(m>8\), then
\[
\#\{0\le r<99:V_x(r)=m\}\le9. \tag{8}
\]
Indeed, partition the 99 values of \(r\) into the nine non-carry columns \(u=0,1,\ldots,8\), each containing \(r=10t+u\) for \(0\le t\le9\), and the carry column \(u=9\), containing \(r=10t+9\) for \(0\le t\le8\). In a fixed non-carry column \(u\), the equation
\[
V_x(10t+u)=x+t+u=m
\]
has at most one solution \(t\). Thus the nine non-carry columns contribute at most nine occurrences. The carry-column values are all at most 8: indeed,
\[
V_x(10t+9)=(x+t+9)\bmod(x+t+1),
\]
and because the numerator is \((x+t+1)+8\), this remainder is at most 8. Therefore the carry column contributes no occurrence of \(m>8\), proving (8).

We will also need the sharper observation that if
\[
8<m\le x,
\]
then among the first 99 positions, \(m\) occurs at most once. To see this, suppose \(V_x(r)=m\). A carry-column value cannot equal \(m\), since it is at most 8. In a non-carry position, writing \(r=10t+u\), we have
\[
m=x+t+u.
\]
But \(m\le x\) and \(t,u\ge0\), so equality forces \(m=x\), \(t=0\), and \(u=0\). Thus the only possible position is \(r=0\), and consequently
\[
\#\{0\le r<99:V_x(r)=m\}\le1
\quad(8<m\le x). \tag{9}
\]

Third, the value 8 occurs at least nine times among the first 99 positions:
\[
\#\{0\le r<99:V_x(r)=8\}\ge9. \tag{10}
\]
For \(x\ge9\), all nine carry positions
\[
r=9,19,29,\ldots,89
\]
have \(x+t\ge8\), so (4) says that all nine give the value 8. For the remaining finite cases \(0\le x\le8\), direct substitution in (5) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
x&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline
\#\{r<99:V_x(r)=8\}&10&10&10&10&10&10&10&10&10.
\end{array}
\]
Thus (10) holds in every case.

We next include the final position \(r=99\) of a block. Put
\[
x=s(q),\qquad y=s(q+1).
\]
Since
\[
s(100q+99)=s(q)+18=x+18
\]
and
\[
100q+99+1=100(q+1),\qquad s(100(q+1))=s(q+1)=y,
\]
we have
\[
a(100q+99)=(x+18)\bmod y. \tag{11}
\]
Here \(y>0\), because \(q+1>0\) and every positive integer has a positive digit sum. We also have
\[
y=s(q+1)\le s(q)+1=x+1. \tag{12}
\]
For completeness, inequality (12) follows from the usual carry analysis. If the final digit of \(q\) is at most 8, adding 1 merely raises that digit by 1, so the digit sum rises by exactly 1. If the final digit is 9, adding 1 changes that 9 to 0 and carries into the quotient obtained by deleting the final digit; applying the same argument recursively to that quotient shows that the total new digit sum is at most the old digit sum plus 1. This induction also covers an arbitrary string of trailing 9’s.

We can now prove the central block estimates. For every \(q\),
\[
\#\{0\le r<100:a(100q+r)=8\}\ge9, \tag{13}
\]
because the first 99 positions already contain at least nine 8’s by (6) and (10); the last position can only add another occurrence.

On the other hand, for every fixed \(m\ne8\),
\[
\#\{0\le r<100:a(100q+r)=m\}\le9. \tag{14}
\]
We split into cases.

If \(m<8\), the first 99 positions contribute at most eight by (7), and the single last position contributes at most one. Hence the total is at most nine.

The case \(m=8\) is excluded.

Suppose \(m>8\). If \(m\le x\), the first 99 positions contribute at most one by (9), while the last position contributes at most one, so the total is at most two, hence at most nine.

Finally, suppose \(m>x\). The first 99 positions contribute at most nine by (8). The last position cannot contribute at all. Indeed, by (11), (12), and positivity of \(y\),
\[
a(100q+99)=(x+18)\bmod y<y\le x+1.
\]
Since \(m>x\) and these are integers, \(x+1\le m\), and therefore the last value is strictly less than \(m\). This proves (14) in all cases.

We pass from one block to arbitrary initial intervals. By summing (14) over the \(q\) complete blocks
\[
[0,99],[100,199],\ldots,[100(q-1),100q-1],
\]
we obtain, for \(m\ne8\),
\[
C_m(100q)\le9q. \tag{15}
\]
Likewise, summing (13) gives
\[
C_8(100q)\ge9q. \tag{16}
\]

For an arbitrary \(N\), write by Euclidean division
\[
N=100q+r,
\qquad q=\left\lfloor\frac N{100}\right\rfloor,
\qquad 0\le r<100.
\]
The final incomplete segment has \(r\) positions. Therefore (15) gives
\[
C_m(N)\le9q+r\qquad(m\ne8), \tag{17}
\]
while (16), ignoring any additional 8’s in that final segment, gives
\[
C_8(N)\ge9q. \tag{18}
\]

We now extract the asymptotic consequences. For \(N>0\), using \(N=100q+r\) and \(0\le r\le99\),
\[
\frac{9q+r}{N}
=
\frac9{100}+\frac{91r}{100N}
\le
\frac9{100}+\frac{100}{N}. \tag{19}
\]
(The final constant 100 is deliberately loose; \(91r/100<100\).) Thus, for every \(m\ne8\), equations (17) and (19) imply
\[
\frac{C_m(N)}N\le\frac9{100}+\frac{100}{N}. \tag{20}
\]
Since \(100/N\to0\), it follows that
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_m(N)}N\le\frac9{100}
\qquad(m\ne8). \tag{21}
\]
Explicitly, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), all sufficiently large \(N\) satisfy \(100/N<\varepsilon\), so (20) eventually bounds the ratio by \(9/100+\varepsilon\), which is precisely the required upper bound on its limsup.

Similarly,
\[
\frac{9q}{N}
=
\frac9{100}-\frac{9r}{100N}
\ge
\frac9{100}-\frac9N, \tag{22}
\]
because \(r\le99<100\). Combining (18) and (22),
\[
\frac{C_8(N)}N\ge\frac9{100}-\frac9N. \tag{23}
\]
As \(9/N\to0\), this yields
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_8(N)}N\ge\frac9{100}. \tag{24}
\]
Indeed, (23) actually proves the same lower bound for the liminf: for every \(\varepsilon>0\), the ratio is eventually at least \(9/100-\varepsilon\).

Finally, fix \(m\in\mathbb N\). If \(m=8\), the two limsups being compared are equal. If \(m\ne8\), then (21) and (24) give
\[
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_m(N)}N
\le\frac9{100}
\le
\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{C_8(N)}N.
\]
Thus the limsup asymptotic frequency of the value 8 is at least that of every other value, as claimed.
